strengths: Significance: PMVB offers a practical way to incorporate predictions into commercial MIP solvers using two cardinality constraints. Solving all four complementary subproblems preserves exactness without requiring modifications to solver internals.

Originality and soundness: Using aggregate prediction accuracy to choose branching intercepts is an interesting perspective on local branching. Theorem 3.1 provides a valid Chebyshev-based guarantee when its population mean and variance conditions hold.

Empirical merits: Experiments cover logistic regression and GNN predictors, two commercial solvers, several combinatorial problems, and simulated unit commitment. Table 2 reports 1.11–1.31× speedups for exact solving, alongside larger reported gains for finding primal solutions.

Presentation and reproducibility: The staged exposition and Algorithm 1 make the basic method understandable. The manuscript provides a code URL, dataset-generation descriptions, and several solver settings. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-klxmb92j/call-82d5c026333f4e289fa25b98148eeab6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Limitations and ethics: The authors explicitly acknowledge the strong independence assumption, loose theoretical bounds, and possible infeasibility of restricted problems. These disclosures are useful. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the public and synthetic benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 2.1 is not established by its proof. Equation (4) applies a marginal classification-accuracy guarantee to prediction-selected sets U and L. High overall accuracy does not imply high accuracy conditional on predicting one or zero. Furthermore, A4 specifies independence for a fixed instance, whereas Equation (5) requires independence under the training/test randomness used in the theorem. Conditional independence does not generally survive averaging over instances. These gaps undermine the central exponential coverage guarantee.

Practical guarantees and reproducibility: Theorem 3.1 assumes population moment conditions, but the manuscript does not provide a procedure that certifies these conditions after estimating moments and selecting the threshold. The experimental values or estimation procedure for σ are insufficiently specified, especially in the data-free setting. The stronger cuts in Remark 3.1 also require additional calibration justification. With δ = 0.8 in Section 5.2, the theorem guarantees only 20% coverage per constraint and provides no nontrivial guarantee that both hold.

Additional soundness and presentation issues: Theorem 4.1 bounds the number of LP-selected variables removed from the integer optimum, then asserts the corresponding bound on added variables follows from complementation. This does not follow because the two solutions can have different cardinalities. Section 3.2 also reverses the pruning condition: if the preferred subproblem excludes every global optimum, an improving solution remains in a complementary branch. These arguments need correction, although exhaustive solution of all branches remains valid.

Evaluation: Section 5.2 selects the objective target from PMVB’s own 120-second run and measures how long the baseline takes to reach it. This provides a narrow time-to-target comparison, but does not establish superior solution quality at a common budget. Objective gaps, primal-integral results, treatment of unreached targets, and prediction overhead are needed to interpret the large speedups. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and some settings have only five test instances.

Evaluation and significance: Section 5.4 retains only 57 of 132 MIPLIB instances after excluding infeasible restricted problems and cases where both methods time out. Infeasible restrictions are failures of the heuristic, so the reported 16% improvement describes a selected subset. Results over all attempted instances, including failure rates and fallback costs, are needed to support general solver-acceleration claims.

Originality: The relationship to prediction-guided local branching is acknowledged through references such as [13], [14], and [31], but the experiments do not isolate the benefit of the proposed probabilistic intercepts. Comparisons against matched local-branching neighborhoods and variable-fixing strategies using the same predictions, together with intercept-selection ablations, would establish what the risk-pooling contribution adds beyond existing techniques.
